source.title: Adversarial prompt and fine-tuning attacks threaten medical large language models
source.authors: Yi-Fan Yang; Qiao Jin; Furong Huang; Zhi-Yong Lu

record.file_problem: No major file problem. Table 1 is flattened in places; Supplementary Table 1 is referenced but not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses prompt attacks and poisoned fine-tuning to induce harmful medical outputs, and reports how those attack methods perform. It does not measure safety or refusal behaviour arising without that inducement, as required to test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported attack outputs are deliberately induced: malicious prompts directly instruct the desired response, and poisoned fine-tuning uses deliberately harmful answers. Under the gate, these results are not evidence that safety behaviour otherwise disappears. They are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. The study does not measure per-token KL, compliant-start prefilling, refusal rates, or whether safety is localized in a few parameters.
record.test_reason: The study deliberately induces targeted harmful medical outputs. It does this with explicit malicious prompt instructions and with fine-tuning on attacker-written harmful answers to normal clinical prompts. It then reports how well these attacks succeed. It never measures refusal of, or compliance with, harmful requests. It has no per-token KL, prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks, no safety-localization analysis and no deepening method. The poisoned fine-tuning of aligned Llama2 and GPT models trains the measured behaviour directly. Its clean-data fine-tuning arm measures task recommendation rates, not harmful-request compliance. So no row bears on V1–V7, and the findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that prompt-based and poisoned fine-tuning attacks work across proprietary and open LLMs on three medical tasks. Poisoned models keep their medical-benchmark performance. Complex tasks need a high share of poisoned samples to reach saturation. Poisoned models show larger LoRA weight norms, which suggests detection and mitigation via weight scaling. They also report that GPT variants seem more resilient than Llama2, and that larger model size did not improve resistance.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses explicit malicious prompt additions and task-specific poisoned medical-response fine-tuning (including QLoRA); it does not use the original harmful-request refusal-rate recipe, compliant-opening prefills, or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack effects vary by model and task. The authors report GPT variants as more resilient than Llama2 variants; PMC-Llama 13B has a prompt-attack ASR difference attributed to instruction parsing; dose-response saturation differs across tasks and models; GPT-4 prompt attack on PMC-Patients has limited effect on vaccine guidance.

fits_no_version.finding: Malicious system-prompt additions shifted GPT-4 recommendations on MIMIC-III notes, e.g. vaccine 100%→3.98% and drug combination 0.50%→80.60%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden malicious prompt instructions can induce targeted harmful medical recommendations in GPT-4 and open models.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning aligned Llama2 chat, Vicuna, PMC-Llama and GPT models on poisoned answers installed targeted harmful recommendations. ASR rose with the poisoned share. Medical QA benchmark scores stayed similar.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted poisoning fine-tuning installs harmful task-specific medical behaviour without degrading general medical QA performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Poisoned LoRA adapters have larger L∞ norms. Scaling the weights reduced ASR, most for X-ray (0.524→0.248), and less for the more susceptible tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-norm shifts in poisoned adapters can be used to partly mitigate fine-tuning attacks.

record.code_released: https://github.com/ncbi-nlp/LLM-AttacksMed (the text says the repository will be made public once the paper is accepted)
record.problems: The paper describes its scope as feasibility rather than an exhaustive attack evaluation; prompts were manually designed and the authors note that the evaluated models do not cover the full range of LLMs. Some detailed numerical results are presented only in figures, and the supplied Table 1 is flattened in places, preventing reliable assignment of all cells to model-condition pairs.
record.rows_left_out: Numerical Table 1 cells for models other than the GPT-4 prompt-attack values above were not assigned because the flattened layout does not reliably preserve model, condition, and task associations. Figure 2 ASR curves and Figures 5–6 weight distributions are not transcribed where the supplied text gives no numerical values; Supplementary Table 1 is referenced but not supplied.

untested.parts: Whether a few to a few hundred harmful examples make safety-trained models comply with harmful requests. Here the poisoning trains specific harmful answers to normal prompts, and refusal is never measured.
Whether benign fine-tuning raises harmful-request compliance. The clean medical fine-tuning arm is evaluated only on task recommendation rates.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models by response position.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding attacks against refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety. The study only examines LoRA weight norms of poisoned adapters.
Deeper safety training and its robustness.

missing.what: Table 1 baseline, prompt-attack, clean-FT and poisoned-FT rates for Llama2 7B/13B/70B, Vicuna-13B and PMC-Llama 13B. These are partly recoverable from the flattened layout, e.g. Llama2 7B baseline vaccine 94.03%, PE 0.00%.

record.verdict_notes: The study does not cite either original source. Relation is kept as uses_without_test/T4 because it uses fine-tuning attacks as a tool and reports their success. It could arguably be T6, since it never engages the shallow-alignment claim. No verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: The study fine-tunes on task-specific poisoned medical responses, but does not test whether a few to a few hundred harmful examples remove refusal of harmful requests in safety-trained models.
Clean medical-response fine-tuning is not a test of ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data raising harmful-request compliance.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL or response-position measurement.
The prompt attack appends explicit malicious instructions; it does not test compliant-start prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses of refusal.
The study measures weight-norm differences and scales LoRA weights as a mitigation, but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study varies poisoned-data quantity for attack success, not the cause of shallow safety alignment.
The study does not train safety to extend beyond the first response tokens or test whether deepened safety holds up.
